newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open flat, pare overnight losses.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open flat, pare overnight losses.

text.p: U.S. government securities opened unchanged on Thursday after overseas traders ran out of fresh reasons to sell, analysts said.

With a light schedule of economic data on Thursday, bears were reined in a bit after Wednesday's selloff briefly spilled over into Tokyo. But analysts said a heavier calendar of corporate issues overnight could add to supply, causing problems.
"There have been a couple of European deals. It hasn't had much effect on Treasuries," said Mike Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.

"I think the supply issue is still weighing a little bit on the market here," Strauss said, adding that retail follow through after the surprisingly strong auction of five-year Treasury notes on Wednesday was minimal.
The T-bond opened unchanged at 98-17/32, yielding 6.74 percent. The 10-year note was also steady at 101-9/32, with a yield of 6.45 percent.
The only numbers of note on Thursday come at 0830 EDT. Jobless claims from last week are seen falling 7,000 to 340,000. The APICS business outlook index for June is also due.
Data this week is not bending the outlook for steady Federal Reserve policy at the July 1-2 FOMC meeting.

But the market is hankering for a first look at June data, with numbers such as Wednesday's 4.4 percent jump in home resales in May possibly foreshadowing a pickup in economic activity soon, analysts said.

"It's really just a series of minor numbers today. The big events are all next week ... the first major tranches of data for June, so that is really what people are looking to now," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co Inc.

Friday's final revision to first-quarter gross domestic product is a small hurdle, with forecasters pointing to an upward adjustment of 0.1 percent to the roaring 5.9 percent growth rate already reported.
But in addition to the Fed's two-day meeting starting Tuesday, the focus is on Tuesday's National Association of Purchasing Management index for June.
Most importantly perhaps, the June payroll report comes on Thursday, one day too late for the central bankers to incorporate into their interest rate talks.
In other trade, the five-year note was off 4/32 in early Thursday trade, standing at 99-19/32 and yielding 6.35 percent. The three-year was off 2/32 at 100-14/32, with a yield of 6.20 percent.
In bills, both the three-month and six-month were up one basis point, standing at 4.98 percent and 5.04 percent, respectively.
